name: Lorlatinib
drug_class: ALK and ROS1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (third generation, macrocyclic)

discovery.by: Pfizer La Jolla (Ted Johnson and colleagues)
discovery.note: A macrocyclic ALK/ROS1 inhibitor designed for blood–brain barrier penetration and activity against resistance mutations including G1202R.

tagline: Macrocyclic ALK inhibitor built to reach the brain and overcome resistance mutations
summary: Lorlatinib is a third-generation macrocyclic ALK and ROS1 inhibitor with high brain penetration and activity against most ALK resistance mutations, including G1202R. It is used first-line and after other ALK inhibitors in ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, where long-term follow-up of the CROWN trial showed unusually durable disease control.
mechanism: The macrocyclic structure constrains the molecule in its bioactive conformation, improving potency and metabolic stability and lowering P-glycoprotein efflux, so it penetrates the central nervous system.
Lorlatinib binds the ATP pocket of wild-type and mutant ALK, including solvent-front G1202R that resists second-generation inhibitors. Compound ALK mutations can still confer resistance.
uses: ALK-positive metastatic NSCLC, first-line or after earlier ALK inhibitors

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Pfizer reports PF-06463922 as a brain-penetrant macrocyclic ALK/ROS1 inhibitor (J Med Chem, Cancer Cell).

history.title: Accelerated approval
history.detail: FDA approves lorlatinib for ALK-positive NSCLC after progression on other ALK inhibitors.

history.title: CROWN
history.detail: CROWN shows superior progression-free survival over crizotinib first-line.

history.title: First-line approval
history.detail: FDA approves lorlatinib for previously untreated ALK-positive NSCLC.

history.title: Five-year CROWN
history.detail: Five-year data show about 60% of patients on lorlatinib remain progression-free.

pk.half_life: about 24 hours (single dose); shorter on repeat dosing due to autoinduction
pk.metabolism: hepatic CYP3A4 and UGT1A4; CYP3A inducer

serious: CNS effects including psychosis and seizures
severe hepatotoxicity with strong CYP3A inducers

facts: Lipid elevations are so common that monitoring and statin therapy are part of routine management.
